# **Mapping potential habitat for the Strange-tailed Tyrant (*Alectrurus risora*): a spatially validated Random Forest model** 

# **Report summary**

This study mapped potential habitat suitability for the Strange-tailed Tyrant (*Alectrurus risora*) in northeastern Argentina using a reproducible workflow combining GBIF occurrence records, Google Earth Engine and R. Occurrences were filtered to retain one presence per 1-km grid cell, resulting in 476 presences. We used six predictors based on the ecological needs of the species: grasslands cover, tree cover, herbaceous and wetland proportions, annual mean temperature, annual precipitation, and precipitation seasonality. 952 pseudoabsences were samples outside of occupied cells. 

For the Species Distribution Model (SDM), we used a Random Forest model which was tuned using internal spatial validation and was further evaluated on 75 km blocks. The evaluation of the model gave a ROC-AUC of 0.849 and a PR-AUC of 741, surpassing by far the precision-recall baseline of 0.330. At an internally selected threshold of 0.202, sensitivity was 85.2% and specificity was 63.5%. Approximately 59,235 km², or 28.02% of the modeled area, were classified as potentially suitable.

The resulting continuous and binary maps provide a preliminary basis for targeting field surveys and supporting regional conservation assessments. Interpretation remains conditional on occurrence sampling bias, pseudoabsence selection, historical climate predictors and a single spatial evaluation partition. Predicted suitability does not establish occupancy, and transferability to future conditions has not been assessed.

# **Introduction and objectives**

The Strange-tailed Tyrant (*Alectrurus risora*) is a grassland-specialist bird associated with savannas and wet grasslands in northeastern Argentina and southern Paraguay. Its dependence on suitable grassland structure makes it relevant for conservation planning in landscapes affected by agricultural management and habitat modification. Field research in Formosa demonstrated that females avoided nesting in recently burned grassland and progressively returned during subsequent breeding seasons, highlighting the importance of vegetation recovery and fire management for breeding habitat availability (Di Giacomo et al., 2011).

Identifying potentially suitable areas can help direct surveys beyond known occurrence sites. Species distribution modeling provides a framework for relating occurrence records to environmental conditions and predicting habitat suitability across a defined region. In this project, grassland, herbaceous wetland and tree-cover proportions were selected to represent landscape composition and openness. Annual mean temperature, annual precipitation and precipitation seasonality were included as candidate predictors of broader climatic conditions. These variables describe regional environmental gradients but do not directly capture vegetation height, grazing intensity, fire history or breeding success.

The main objective was to develop a reproducible, spatially evaluated model of potential habitat suitability for *A. risora* within an occurrence based calibration area encompassing northeastern Argentina and adjacent areas. The specific objectives were to:

1. Integrate GBIF occurrences with remotely sensed land-cover and climatic predictors on a common 1 km grid.  
2. Fit a Random Forest model using presences and sampled pseudoabsences, with spatial separation between training and evaluation data.  
3. Assess predictive discrimination using ROC-AUC and PR-AUC, alongside threshold-dependent classification metrics.  
4. Produce continuous suitability and binary habitat maps to support field-survey planning and preliminary regional conservation assessments.  
   

# **Study area and data source**

The study covered an occurrence-based region encompassing northeastern Argentina and adjacent areas. The calibration area (M) was delineated by constructing a convex hull around the retained occurrence locations and adding a 50 km buffer. This provided an operational approximation of the area potentially accessible to the species. The area with complete environmental data covered approximately 211,383 km².

Occurrence data were obtained from GBIF and retained with geographic coordinates and observation dates. The processed dataset contained 751 distinct locations. After alignment with the environmental grid, one occurrence was selected per occupied cell using a fixed random seed, yielding 476 presence records. The original download is identified by DOI: [https\://doi.org/10.15468/dl.xsq88m](https://doi.org/10.15468/dl.xsq88m).

Six environmental predictors were assembled to represent landscape composition and broad climatic conditions.

| Predictor | Description and units | Source |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Grassland cover | Proportion of grassland within a cell (0–1) | ESA WorldCover 2021 v200 |
| Tree cover | Proportion of tree cover within a cell (0–1) | ESA WorldCover 2021 v200 |
| Herbaceous wetland cover | Proportion of herbaceous wetland within a cell (0–1) | ESA WorldCover 2021 v200 |
| Annual mean temperature  (BIO1) | Mean annual temperature, °C | WorldClim V1 BIO |
| Annual precipitation  (BIO12) | Annual precipitation total, mm | WorldClim V1 BIO |
| Precipitation seasonality  (BIO15) | Coefficient of variation of monthly precipitation | WorldClim V1 BIO |

Land-cover predictors were derived from the 10 m ESA WorldCover classification for 2021 (Zanaga et al., 2022). Binary indicators of grassland, tree cover and herbaceous wetland were aggregated into fractional cover layers in Google Earth Engine. Climatic predictors were obtained from the WorldClim V1 BIO collection (Hijmans et al., 2005). These layers represent historical climatic conditions rather than weather during the occurrence-recording period.

The six predictors were exported from Google Earth Engine as a multiband GeoTIFF and processed in R using **terra** package. They were reprojected with bilinear interpolation onto a common 1,000 × 1,000 m grid in WGS 84 / UTM zone 21S (EPSG:32721) and masked to M. Consequently, the final land-cover fractions represent resampled estimates. All 476 selected presences had complete values for the six predictors.

# **Methodology**

A Random Forest model was fitted using six environmental predictors, 476 presences and 952 pseudoabsences. Samples were divided into training and evaluation sets using 75 km spatial blocks. Model settings and the classification threshold were selected through spatial validation within the training set.

Performance was assessed on reserved evaluation blocks. The ROC curve shows the relationship between sensitivity and the false-positive rate across thresholds; ROC-AUC summarizes discrimination between presences and pseudoabsences. The precision–recall curve shows the trade-off between detecting recorded presences and the proportion of predicted positives that are recorded presences. Its reference baseline was 0.330, the presence fraction in the evaluation set.

The evaluated model produced a continuous habitat-suitability map at 1 km resolution. A threshold of 0.202, selected by maximizing sensitivity plus specificity during internal validation, classified cells as potentially suitable or unsuitable. These maps represent predicted environmental suitability, not confirmed occupancy.

# **Results**

The Random Forest achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.849 and a PR-AUC of 0.741 on the spatially reserved evaluation set. PR-AUC exceeded the reference baseline of 0.330, indicating discrimination above the random-ranking expectation for this sample composition (Figure 1). At the selected threshold of 0.202, sensitivity was 85.2%, specificity 63.5%, and precision 53.5%. The model correctly classified 121 of 142 presences and 183 of 288 pseudoabsences.

![][image1]

**Figure 1**. ROC and precision–recall curves for the reserved spatial evaluation set. Dashed lines indicate random-ranking reference levels: the diagonal in ROC space and a precision of 0.330 in PR space.

The continuous map showed spatial variation in habitat suitability, while the binary map identified approximately 59,235 km² as potentially suitable, representing 28.02% of the modeled area (Figure 2). These estimates refer to the calibration area and do not incorporate a permanent-water mask. 

![][image2]

**Figure 2\.** Predicted habitat suitability for Alectrurus risora: (Left) continuous suitability scores and (Right) binary classification using a threshold of 0.202. Predictions are presented at 1-km resolution.

# **Conclusion**

The model provides a reproducible regional assessment of potential habitat for *Alectrurus risora*, supporting the identification of areas for targeted field surveys. Spatial evaluation indicated useful predictive discrimination, although results remain conditional on occurrence sampling, pseudoabsence selection and the chosen spatial partition. The maps represent potential environmental suitability rather than confirmed occupancy and should be complemented by field verification before informing site-specific conservation decisions.
